title: Laylat al-Qadr
hook: in Ramadan's last nights, Muslims pray for forgiveness on the Night of Power (Quran 97)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Forgiveness Sunday, a line of bows before Lent. Your line was forgive me. Today, the last of these days of forgiveness: a single night, hidden somewhere near the end of Ramadan.

It's past midnight near the end of Ramadan, and the mosque is still lit. Some people stand in prayer. Some sit against the wall with the Qur'an open on their knees. Some have brought blankets and will stay until dawn. At home, others pray quietly in a back room while the house sleeps. Nobody knows for certain which of these nights is the one they're looking for. That's part of it. The night has a name, and a whole short chapter of the Qur'an to itself. Laylat al-Qadr: the Night of Power.
screen: `PAST MIDNIGHT, STILL LIT.` → `WHICH NIGHT IS IT?` → `THE NIGHT OF POWER.`

segments.voice: First, what the Qur'an says. Surah ninety-seven is short. In Pickthall's translation it opens: "Lo! We revealed it on the Night of Power." Muslims understand it to be the Qur'an, first sent down on this night. Then a startling comparison: "The Night of Power is better than a thousand months." Second, how it ends. The angels and the Spirit come down, the chapter says, and the night is "Peace until the rising of the dawn." Not a night of fear or judgment: a night of peace. Third, the hiding. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, told his followers to seek the night in the last nights of Ramadan, the odd-numbered ones, according to a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari. That hadith gives no single date, so people keep watch across several nights. Some readers see the hiding as a mercy of its own: it keeps people praying longer. Fourth, the question his wife asked. In a hadith recorded by al-Tirmidhi, Aisha asks him what she should say if she knows which night it is. He teaches her a short supplication, in paraphrase: God, you are the one who pardons, and you love to pardon, so pardon me. Of all the things to ask for on a night better than a thousand months, the answer he gives is forgiveness.
screen: `WE REVEALED IT ON THIS NIGHT.` · `BETTER THAN A THOUSAND MONTHS.` · `PEACE UNTIL THE DAWN.` · `YOU LOVE TO PARDON, SO PARDON ME.` · then, large: `THE NIGHT OF POWER.`

segments.voice: Let these minutes be a small night watch, whatever the hour, and bring to mind the first thing you'd ask to be forgiven for, without explaining or defending it. Then, in your own way, ask: if you pray, with the words of your own tradition, or, if you're Muslim, the words the Prophet taught Aisha. If you don't pray, simply let yourself want it to be let go, and stay with that wanting.
Laylat al-Qadr. The Night of Power, in the last nights of Ramadan, when the Qur'an was first revealed and Muslims keep watch and ask forgiveness. Today's word.
Your line: the night of power. A night of peace, until the dawn. That's day nine hundred ninety-six.

chat.meaning: Surah 97 calls the Night of Power better than a thousand months, and peace until dawn. Its date is hidden, so people keep watch.

notes: Pickthall 1930 wording of 97:1, 97:3 and 97:5 (where '(The night is)' precedes 'Peace until the rising of the dawn'): verify exactly.
Bukhari 2017 (seek it in the odd nights of the last ten of Ramadan): confirm number; the voice says 'the last nights ... the odd-numbered ones' without the number ten.
Tirmidhi 3513 (Aisha's question; the supplication Allahumma innaka 'afuwwun tuhibbul-'afwa fa'fu 'anni) is paraphrased, not quoted.
'Some scholars have said the hiding is itself a mercy': soft attribution; confirm it is fairly represented, or cut.
Gloss of 'afw as 'pardon in a full sense, letting a wrong go entirely' is a lexical claim; a Keeper should confirm or trim to 'pardon'.
'Muslims understand it to be the Qur'an, first sent down on this night': standard reading of 97:1 with 2:185; confirm wording.
Hook's scene (mosque lit, people staying until dawn) is descriptive of practice, not a claim about all Muslims.
Index hook says 'many Muslims'; the script hook field omits 'many' per the claims rule (index unchanged).
